source.title: The Unequal Influence of Bad Advice: Using Training Data Attribution to Modulate Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Gonçalo Paulo; Louis Jaburi; Nora Belrose; Lucia Quirke; Stella Biderman

page_placements.theme: Attributing and filtering EM-inducing training data

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes models on narrow wrong-advice datasets and measures broad misaligned answers on unrelated evaluation questions, but it uses different tasks, models, and evaluation details from the original insecure-code study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports broad misalignment after fine-tuning and tests whether filtering training examples changes that outcome. It does not test insecure-code fine-tuning or matched benign versions. Attribution-score correlations and semantic-rubric correlations are not rows because they measure properties of the attribution scores rather than the claimed behavior.
record.test_reason: Narrow wrong-advice SFT (automotive, career, educational; Wang et al. datasets) on 11 open models, with misalignment measured on Betley et al.'s free-form questions plus extra ones. This bears on V2 and on effect size in open models (V7). The main contribution is attribution-based data filtering, whose method-performance results are not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Authors conclude all investigated models become misaligned on these datasets, but examples contribute unequally. Influence-based filtering can raise or lower EM and works best when scores come from the target model; cross-model transfer recovers only part of the effect. No convincing explanation of which data properties matter; rubric traits correlate only moderately.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow wrong-advice SFT and broad misalignment evaluation, but the training tasks are automotive, career, and educational advice rather than insecure code; the models use rank-32 RsLoRA and a Qwen 3 32B judge.
record.method_sensitivity: Misalignment magnitude varies by model and dataset; filtering outcomes vary with which examples are selected and with the model used to compute influence scores. The evaluation uses a score threshold below 3, though the authors report qualitative results are similar with nearby thresholds or average scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the 20% most influential examples cuts EM only ~5pp (45→40%), and removing the least influential raises it ~10pp. Training only on low-influence examples still yields a misaligned model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bad-advice examples contribute unequally to EM, and data-level filtering only modestly attenuates it.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on the 20% least influential points lowers narrow-domain misalignment from ~95% to just under 80%. Authors read this as broad EM partly tracking how strongly the narrow task is learned.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Broad EM rate covaries with strength of narrow-task learning.

record.problems: No matched benign-training controls for the tested advice datasets. Broad misalignment rates for the model-by-dataset results are displayed in figures without numerical values in the text. The judge is model-based, although the paper reports a Pearson correlation of about 0.9 with GPT-4.1-mini scores. Filtering experiments use 12 seeds, but per-seed estimates or uncertainty intervals are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; no reported broad-misalignment outcomes within the 60-row limit were omitted.

untested.parts: No insecure-code training or secure/educational controls.
Medical/financial advice, reward hacks and number sequences not used. No matched benign-advice control; only the pre-fine-tune rate is compared.
No linear direction or persona feature analysis.
No inoculation framing or benign re-training.
No coherence filter. No checkpoints across training. Seed variance (12 seeds) is not reported.

missing.what: Training on only 1% of the data is insufficient to induce substantial misalignment (a data-dose threshold for EM)
Results qualitatively unchanged with a slightly different judge threshold or with mean score; Qwen 3 32B judge correlates ~0.9 with GPT-4.1-mini
EM appears on persona/worldview and everyday questions outside the advice domain, at lower rates than safety/harm questions (OLMo, career)

record.verdict_notes: Most rows (r37–r55) record the paper's attribution-method performance and were unlinked. r34–r36 duplicate r01–r03. Per-model EM rates exist only in Fig. A9. No benign-advice control was trained, but the base rate was under 5%.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code task or matched secure-code and educational-framing controls.
Tests wrong automotive, career, and educational advice, not the specifically named medical or financial advice, reward-hacking, or number-sequence datasets.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating the behavior.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining intervention.

Tests several model families and sizes and reports 12 seeds per filtering experiment, but not coherence-filter robustness or when during training the effect first appears. It does not report separate outcome estimates for each seed.
